does flame spread faster in microgravity.answer: In microgravity, materials with adequate ventilation may burn more readily compared to normal gravity under identical conditions [1]. Specifically, a microgravity concurrent-flow flame reaches nearly steady-state with a convex base, whereas a normal-gravity flame is much longer, sootier, has a concave base, and continues to accelerate over the available fuel length [2]. Additionally, certain fuels that cannot burn in a downward (opposed-flow) configuration in normal gravity will support opposed-flow burning in microgravity [2].

how does smoke differ in microgravity (s.answer: In microgravity, the absence of strong buoyancy-induced flows and reduced velocities/mixing lead to higher vapor concentrations and longer smoke residence times near the source [1][2]. These conditions promote increased smoke particle growth through nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, resulting in larger smoke particles and liquid aerosol droplets compared to normal gravity (1-g), with a corresponding decrease in particle number density for the same mass of smoke [1]. These microgravity-induced changes in particle size distribution and number density affect the response of smoke detectors and can potentially prevent an alarm when exposed to the smoke [1].

This promotes particle growth via nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, resulting in substantially larger smoke particles (and larger liquid aerosol droplet sizes) compared to normal gravity (1g), along with a corresponding decrease in particle number density for the same mass of smoke [1][2]. In the SAME-2 microgravity reflight experiment, the majority of average smoke particle sizes from tested spacecraft materials were found to range between 200 nm and 400 nm, with quiescent flow cases producing even larger particles [3].

what is known about fires at moon-base a.answer: In microgravity tests exploring proposed NASA atmospheres with 34% oxygen and pressures around 0.56 atm (8.2 psia), common plastics such as PMMA (emulated via ethylene/N2 fuel mixtures with heats of combustion around 22–24 kJ/g) can steadily burn [2][3]. For these conditions, flames reach steady state or quasi-steady state after approximately 80 to 100 seconds [2][3]. Additionally, tests at 34% oxygen showed that all examined flames reached steady burning, whereas flames at lower oxygen concentrations (such as 21%) led to self-extinction in less than about 25 seconds [2]. Furthermore, extended lunar-surface missions will require fire detection systems specifically designed to resist influence from lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources [1].
